title: Scarlet Mimic
summary: Scarlet Mimic is a long-running espionage cluster that public reporting describes as active since at least 2015, with victims concentrated among political, diplomatic, government and human-rights organisations. Its best-known trait is name confusion: researchers reported that its tooling was designed to make intrusions look like the work of unrelated actors, using file names, paths and artefacts associated with a different well-known malware family. Reporting also describes targeting of computers and mobile devices, including attempts to install monitoring software on Android phones through links sent in chat and email. Because the operators plant false clues deliberately, attribution of any single incident is fragile, and public reporting presents sponsorship as a low-confidence judgement. Analysis must rest on behaviour across the whole intrusion.

beginner.definition: Scarlet Mimic is a spying group that public reports say has operated since around 2015. It targets political groups, government offices and human rights organisations. It is known for making its attacks look like the work of a different group. That makes its activity hard to link to any one sponsor with confidence.
beginner.whyItMatters: When an intruder hides behind another group's name, responders can chase the wrong explanation. That wastes time and can lead to the wrong conclusion. For people in political or human rights work, a wrong accusation can also cause real harm. Careful, evidence-based analysis protects both the investigation and the people involved. This is a lesson about patience, not speed.
howItWorks: The attackers choose targets whose messages, contacts and documents carry political or diplomatic value.
They send links or files in email and chat that appear to come from a trusted contact.
The harmful program is built so its file names and traces resemble another known group's tools.
Analysts who only see those traces may blame the wrong actor and miss the real one.
On phones, links can lead to monitoring software that copies messages, calls and location data.
The stolen material is sent to servers the attackers control, often using ordinary web traffic.
beginner.example: Think of a thief who deliberately leaves a scarf with a rival gang's colours at the scene. The police find it, and the whole case points at the wrong people. Only careful work, such as checking where the scarf was bought, shows the truth. Intrusions can be staged the same way, so a single clue is never proof.
takeaways: Attackers can plant false clues, so one matching detail never proves who is responsible.
Mobile devices need protection too, especially for people whose work attracts attention.
Describe attribution with appropriate uncertainty, because a wrong claim can harm real people.

objectives: Describe Scarlet Mimic and the kinds of organisations its campaigns are reported to target.
Explain the concept of a false flag in intrusion analysis and why it misleads responders.
Explain why attribution should rely on multiple independent evidence sources.
Describe the additional risk that mobile monitoring software creates for targeted individuals.
Discuss how victim profile affects the language used when reporting on an intrusion.
Identify the evidence types that remain useful when an attacker plants misleading artefacts.
